fields.description: You came up the high road at dawn with a tired horse, a light purse and an open mind. Brindlemere is the first town in three days with a bed and a warm meal.

fields.description: A careful man with ink on his cuffs who knows every debt in town and carries the worst of them himself. He is proud of the town's tidy accounts and dislikes being asked about them.
Broad-shouldered, sunburned and blunt. She has hauled the ferry rope since she was twelve and trusts weather more than people.

fields.description: Floury to the elbows even on his day off, gloomy when the wheel is still and ridiculously generous when it turns. The Tambers have milled here for four generations.
Quick-handed, dry-humoured and always smudged with soot. Her forge made the ferry chain, and she is not above reminding people of it.
fields.activity: selling hinges, nails and knives at her stall

fields.description: A small, upright woman with a calm voice and surprising stubbornness. She has polished the silent bell every dawn for twenty-two years and will not discuss why it stopped.
fields.role: Keeper of the Chapel of the Quiet Bell

fields.description: Warm, curious and always mid-sentence. She learned her trade from her grandmother and charges what people can pay, which is often a basket of eggs.
Round, jovial and always polishing the same mug. He knows everyone's business, shares most of it, and has a soft, easily bruised spot for Wren.
Tamsin's nephew: lanky, quick and forever coiling rope. He hears more than he repeats and has good instincts about who is lying.

fields.description: A weathered widower who keeps the lamp lit and the kettle hot. His daughter Nessa is eight and has been ill for three days.

fields.description: A drawstring purse of soft leather.
A canvas rucksack on a leather frame.
A cracked leather satchel with brass buckles, packed and ready.
An iron-bound oak chest under the long table, with two locks.
An old oak chest in the Crooked Kettle's back storeroom, where the inn keeps its spare crockery and whatever guests have left behind.
Oiled wool, patched at the hem, smelling faintly of horse.
A plain linen shirt, soft with years of washing.
Resoled once; still watertight.
Hard-wearing, dyed the brown of old bark.
A plain eating knife with a bone handle.
A pierced-tin lantern with a horn window and a stub of candle.
Two pints, stitched leather.
A coil of thin but strong hemp rope, a little frayed at the ends.
Salt pork, hard cheese and a heel of bread, wrapped in cloth.
A palm-sized book with a stub of lead pencil.
Worn, comfortable and just a size too big for the horse.
Willow bark, yarrow and honey in a waxed jar, sealed with a cloth tie.
A hand-dressed grinding stone, almost the right size, lying face-up in the nettles. Heavy.
The mill's runner stone, split edge to edge.
A fifty-pound sack, stamped with the Tamber mark.
A large vellum charter in a dark frame, granting Brindlemere its market and its freedom from the lord's tithes.
A bronze bell, polished at the lip and green in the crown, hanging without a clapper.
A worn floor tile carved with stepping stones across a stream.
A floor tile carved with a flat boat on a rope.
A floor tile carved with three arches.
A heavy cross-peen hammer with a handle gone dark with sweat.
A dappled grey gelding, patient and a little lazy. Stabled behind the Kettle.
A sturdy ash-wood cart with iron-shod wheels. Marta lends it to anyone she trusts and a few people she doesn't.
A flat, broad-beamed ferry hauled along a rope by hand and winch. Fares are paid at the toll-hut.
A broad green valley where the River Wend slows and spreads. Orchards and mill-ponds crowd the near bank; woods and grazing climb the far one.
A market town of grey stone and red tile, about eight hundred souls, built where the high road meets the ferry. Everything in it is a short walk from the square.
A cobbled square with a stone well at its heart. On Marketday the stalls go up before dawn and the whole vale comes to trade.
A leaning, low-beamed inn with a copper kettle hung crooked over the door. Warm, noisy and always smelling of onions and woodsmoke; there are six beds upstairs and a stable yard behind.
The town's broad-windowed meeting hall. The reeve keeps his ledgers here, petitioners queue in the passage, and the framed Charter hangs behind the long table.
A narrow cottage hung with drying bundles of yarrow, mint and willow bark. A kettle is always warm, and the back garden is a tangle of useful weeds.
A small, plain chapel with a square tower and a bell that no one has heard in thirty years. Candles, polished pews and a vestry off the nave smelling of beeswax and old dust.
A smoky, open-fronted forge where hinges, nails, knives and ferry chain come off the anvil. A bench by the door has worn smooth under three generations of loiterers.
A gravel slip, a boathouse and a squat toll-hut at the foot of the town. A flat ferry hauled on a rope crosses the Wend to the far bank in about a quarter of an hour.
A three-storey mill on the river bend, its wheel as tall as a cottage. When it turns, the whole lower town hears the low thrum of the stones.
A grassed-over quarry above the old apple terraces, where the town's first millstones were cut. Rough-hewn blocks still lie in the nettles where the cutters left them.
A lonely stone house across the river where drovers and pilgrims wait for the ferry. A lamp burns in its window every night.
Damp stone steps lead down into a low, cold room that smells of old water and wet stone.

charter.label: A document older than the hall's

fields.description: A waxed leather tube holding a long, folded vellum sealed with the town's first seal.

charter.cue: On a dry ledge, a waxed tube holds a long vellum sealed with the town's first seal: the Founding Charter, in a hand older than the one hanging in Reeve's Hall.

truth.label: What the bell was guarding
truth.cue: The two charters do not say the same thing.
truth.truth: The Charter framed in Reeve's Hall is a copy made from memory after the Great Flood, and it omits the clause that gives the ferry and the mill to the townsfolk in common. Brother Anselm hid the original in the chapel cistern during the flood and silenced the bell so that no one would linger in the vestry; he died before he could tell anyone. Reeve Hollis Garrow found the omission last winter while auditing old tolls. Believing the town had no claim, he has been leasing the ferry fares to a distant lord's steward to pay the town's debt, and he is ashamed of it.

economy.regions.label: Regions (US states, DC and the national baseline)

basis.summary: Rounded, approximate state-level figures compiled from well-known public statistics as recalled; not queried live. Intended as plausible defaults, not as authoritative statistics.
basis.state_income_tax_effective_pct: Approximate effective state income tax as a percent of gross wages for a single filer earning about $60,000 (a middle-income band), after the state standard deduction/exemptions; derived from published 2025 state brackets (Tax Foundation / state revenue departments). Rounded to 0.1. Excludes local income taxes (see local_income_tax_pct_typical) and payroll-type state levies such as CA SDI.
basis.sales_tax_combined_avg_pct: Tax Foundation 2025 combined state plus population-weighted average local sales tax rate; rounded to 0.01. Hawaii and Alaska values are approximations of the GET / local-only rate.
basis.cost_of_living_multiplier: US = 1.00. Approximate from BEA Regional Price Parities (all items, 2022-2023 vintage) smoothed to 2025; rounded to 0.01.
basis.median_rent_cents_per_month: Approximate asking-rent medians for 1BR and 2BR units, a blend of Zumper, Apartment List and HUD FY2025 Fair Market Rent state patterns, rounded to $10. 1BR is the anchor; 2BR is derived as 1BR times a regional ratio (Northeast 1.22, Midwest 1.27, South 1.27, West 1.24; DC uses South) rounded to $10. Statewide medians hide large metro-vs-rural spread.
basis.residential_electricity_cents_per_kwh: EIA Electric Power Monthly, average residential retail price by state, 2024 annual / 2025 year-to-date, rounded to 0.5 cent. Decimal value in cents (not dollars) per kWh. US average is about 17 cents.
basis.minimum_wage_cents_per_hour: Effective statutory floor in 2025 for non-tipped adult workers: the higher of the state rate and the federal $7.25. Where rates vary by locality or employer size (NY, OR, MN) the statewide/largest-area figure is used.

scope.doc: `national` is the single baseline row `us` (multiplier 1.00); the state-only columns are absent on it.

state_income_tax_effective_pct.doc: Single filer at about $60,000, after the state standard deduction; excludes local and payroll levies.

cost_of_living_multiplier.doc: US = 1.00. Applied by the economy pack at pricing time, never baked into rows.

minimum_wage_cents_per_h.doc: Effective 2025 floor, the higher of state and federal.

ak.name: Alaska

az.name: Arizona

de.name: Delaware

fl.name: Florida

hi.name: Hawaii

id.name: Idaho
id.notes: Northern panhandle (north of the Salmon River) is Pacific time; the rest is Mountain.

in.name: Indiana
in.notes: Most of the state is Eastern; the northwest and southwest corners are Central. County income tax is extra (see local_income_tax_pct_typical).

ks.name: Kansas
ks.notes: Four far-western counties are Mountain time.

ky.name: Kentucky
ky.notes: Roughly the western half is Central; the eastern half is Eastern.

mi.name: Michigan
mi.notes: Four Upper Peninsula counties bordering Wisconsin are Central.

mt.name: Montana
mt.notes: No general sales tax; resort-area local taxes exist.

ne.name: Nebraska
ne.notes: The western panhandle is Mountain time.

nh.name: New Hampshire
nh.notes: No tax on wages; the interest and dividends tax was repealed effective 2025. No sales tax.

ny.name: New York
ny.notes: Excludes New York City resident income tax (roughly 3-4% more) and the MCTMT.

nd.name: North Dakota
nd.notes: The southwest corner is Mountain time. Effective income tax is near zero for the middle band (large 0% bracket).

oh.name: Ohio
oh.notes: Municipal income taxes (about 1-2.5%) apply in most cities and are extra.

or.name: Oregon
or.notes: Most of Malheur County is Mountain time. No state sales tax; effective income tax is among the highest for a middle band.

pa.name: Pennsylvania
pa.notes: Local earned-income tax (about 1% typical, Philadelphia 3.75%) is extra.

sd.name: South Dakota
sd.notes: The western half (west of the Missouri River, mostly) is Mountain time.

tn.name: Tennessee
tn.notes: East Tennessee is Eastern time; the rest is Central. No wage income tax.

tx.name: Texas
tx.notes: El Paso and Hudspeth counties are Mountain time.

wa.name: Washington
wa.notes: No wage income tax. Capital-gains excise tax applies only to large gains.

source.reflectsPeriod: 2025-2026 (rates as of late 2025; Fed funds target 3.50-3.75% after the Dec 2025 cut)
source.basis: Rounded typical consumer-finance parameters recalled from Federal Reserve G.19 and H.15, FDIC national rates, Freddie Mac PMMS, Bankrate / Edmunds surveys, CFPB, KFF Employer Health Benefits Survey 2025, Vanguard How America Saves 2025, IRS Rev. Proc. 2024-40 and IRS notices for 2025/2026; not queried live. Treat as plausible defaults.

values.doc: The section as in the source. Keys containing `cents` are integer cents, keys containing `pct` are percent units; ranges are {min, typical, max}.

fed_funds_target_pct.note: Target range after the December 2025 FOMC cut; was 4.25-4.50 for most of H1 2025.

apr_pct.note: Fed G.19 average on accounts assessed interest is ~22%; new-offer averages ~24%; best-credit cards 15-18%, subprime 28-30%.

grace_period_days.note: No interest if the previous balance is paid in full; none on cash advances.

minimum_payment.formula: min(statement_balance + interest + fees, max(floor_cents, ceil(statement_balance * principal_pct / 100 + interest_this_cycle + fees_this_cycle)))

variants.issuer_style: 1% of balance plus interest and fees
2% of balance, no extra interest add-on

minimum_payment.interest_per_cycle: balance * apr_pct / 100 / 12 (monthly periodic rate; issuers use average daily balance with daily rate = apr/365)

late_fee_cents.note: Reg Z safe-harbor amounts for 2025 ($32 first, $43 repeat); the CFPB $8 cap was vacated in April 2025. Issuers commonly charge $30-$41.

cash_advance_fee.note: No grace period; interest starts the same day.

high_yield.note: Online banks; floating with the Fed funds rate.

checking_apy_pct.note: Most checking accounts pay near zero; a few reward accounts pay 3-4% up to a balance cap.

monthly_maintenance.note: Often waived with direct deposit or a minimum balance ($1,000-$1,500).

atm_out_of_network_total.note: Bankrate-style average ~$4.73 (operator surcharge plus bank fee).

overdraft.note: Average ~$27; many banks have cut or eliminated overdraft fees; cap per day typical 3 charges.

auto.payment_formula: payment = P * r / (1 - (1 + r)^-n), r = apr_pct/100/12, n = term_months

apr_pct_30yr_fixed.note: Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year averaged about 6.3-6.9% through 2025; borrowers with lower credit pay more.

pmi_pct_per_year.note: Applies when down payment is under 20%.

property_tax_pct_of_value_per_year.note: Effective rate; varies by state and county.

homeowners_insurance_cents_per_month.note: Higher in hurricane, hail and wildfire areas.

apr_pct.note: Fed G.19 24-month personal loan average ~12%; online lenders 7-36%.

payday.note: High-cost; usually avoided; included for debt-trap scenarios.

investing.title: Investing (index return model, GBM recipe, bonds, cash)

broad_us_equity_index.description: Total-return broad US stock index (S&P 500 style) for seeded price paths; use geometric Brownian motion with these parameters.
broad_us_equity_index.long_run_basis: 1926-2024 nominal total return ~10% geometric, ~12% arithmetic, ~19% volatility; modern-era (post-1990) volatility ~15-17%; the typical 5-year-ahead expectation is lower, ~6-8% nominal.
broad_us_equity_index.gbm_note: S(t+dt) = S(t) * exp((mu - sigma^2/2) dt + sigma sqrt(dt) Z) with mu=0.11, sigma=0.16 per year; use a seeded RNG.

retirement_account_limits_cents.note: IRS limits for 2025; 2026 values as announced in IRS Notice 2025-67 (401(k) $24,500, catch-up $8,000, IRA $7,500).

single.note: KFF 2025: average worker contribution ~$1,440/yr (about 16% of a ~$9,300 premium) for single coverage.

family.note: KFF 2025: average worker contribution ~$6,850/yr (~26% of a ~$27,000 premium).

health_deductible_cents.note: Annual deductible; KFF average single deductible ~ $1,800 in 2025.

employer_match_typical.formula: 50% of the first 6% of pay (3% of pay)

retirement_401k.note: Vanguard How America Saves 2025: average deferral ~7.7% (12% total with employer); most common auto-enroll default 3-4%.

garnishment.note: Federal CCPA limits; not applied by default.

ev_sedan.notes: No oil changes. Many states add an EV registration surcharge of about $100-$250 per year, included in the registration band. Tires wear faster (instant torque, weight).

ev_crossover.name: Electric crossover (Model Y / Equinox EV class)
ev_crossover.notes: Cargo volume with rear seats folded.

motorcycle_standard.name: Motorcycle, standard or cruiser (500-900 cc)
motorcycle_standard.notes: Cargo is saddlebags or a tail bag; a passenger seat is optional. Front/rear tires are replaced separately (rear wears ~2x faster). Helmet laws vary by state.

scooter_150.name: Scooter or moped (50-150 cc)
scooter_150.notes: Under-seat storage about 25-35 L. Mopeds under 50 cc often need no registration or license in some states; top speed 30-60 mph.

bass_boat_outboard.name: Outboard bass boat (18-20 ft, 150-200 hp)

maintenance.engine_service_note: oil, filters and lower-unit gear oil every 100 hours or annually

bass_boat_outboard.notes: Boat state registration usually renews every 1-3 years (annualised here); trailer is registered separately (~$30-$100/year). Price includes motor and trailer. Cruise burn is at planing speed with a normal load.

pontoon_boat.name: Pontoon boat (22-24 ft, 90-150 hp outboard)
pontoon_boat.notes: Capacity plate typically 8-13 persons / 1,500-2,500 lb total.

jet_ski_pwc.name: Personal watercraft / jet ski (1-3 seats)

maintenance.engine_service_note: oil and filter every 50 hours or annually

jet_ski_pwc.notes: Premium-grade fuel recommended by most makers. Price excludes trailer ($800-$2,500).

sailboat_auxiliary.name: Cruising sailboat with auxiliary diesel (30-35 ft)

consumption.note: Displacement hull: motors at hull speed (~6 knots) burning 0.6-1.0 gph; sailing uses no fuel.

maintenance.engine_service_note: oil and filters every 100-150 hours; impeller every 200 hours

sailboat_auxiliary.notes: Documented vessels (US Coast Guard documentation) pay no state registration. A rule of thumb is that ownership costs 10% of value per year. Sleeps 4-6.

atv_utility.name: ATV, utility quad (450-700 cc)
atv_utility.notes: Cargo: front and rear racks, about 40 kg front and 80 kg rear. Many states require an off-highway vehicle (OHV) sticker/permit rather than road registration; helmet and age rules vary.

utv_side_by_side.name: UTV / side-by-side (Ranger / RZR class, 2-4 seats)
utv_side_by_side.notes: Utility models carry a dump bed up to ~450 kg; sport models carry people only. Roll cage and belts required.

dirt_bike_250.name: Dirt bike, 250 cc four-stroke
dirt_bike_250.notes: Competition bikes are not street legal; plated dual-sport bikes use the motorcycle class. Premium fuel with 91+ octane typical.

riding_horse.name: Riding horse
riding_horse.notes: A dappled grey gelding, patient and a little lazy. Stabled behind the Kettle.

two_wheel_cart.name: Two-wheel cart
two_wheel_cart.notes: A sturdy ash-wood cart with iron-shod wheels. Marta lends it to anyone she trusts and a few people she doesn't.

rope_ferry.name: Rope ferry
rope_ferry.notes: A flat, broad-beamed ferry hauled along a rope by hand and winch. Fares are paid at the toll-hut.

source.reflectsPeriod: 2025-2026 (model-year 2025 new prices; used = about 3-5 years old)

basis.prices_and_economy: Typical new MSRP bands, used-market (Edmunds, Kelley Blue Book, NADA) values and EPA fueleconomy.gov combined ratings for representative models, rounded; marine and off-road from manufacturer spec sheets (Mercury, Yamaha, Sea-Doo, Polaris, Honda) and dealer pricing.
basis.insurance: Bankrate / Insurify 2025 average premiums: full coverage about $2,300-$2,700 per year for a clean-record adult, state-minimum liability about $600-$800 per year; EVs are 15-25% higher; boats about 1.5% of value per year; rounded to cents per month.
basis.maintenance: Manufacturer service schedules and AAA / RepairPal cost surveys, rounded.
basis.registration: State DMV fee ranges; actual cost varies by weight, value, age and county.

factors.doc: Factor id to consumption multiplier (>1 burns more). Road: relative to the combined rating; marine: to cruise_planing; off-road: to normal_trail.

road.basis: Multipliers on fuel (or energy) consumed per mile relative to the combined rating; >1 burns more. Rounded rules of thumb from EPA/fueleconomy.gov and AAA tests.
road.note: For EVs the same multipliers apply to kWh per mile (cold weather is harsher: use 1.35; highway 75 mph: 1.30; towing: 2.0).

marine.basis: Multipliers on gallons per hour at planing cruise; rules of thumb from engine makers' fuel curves (Mercury, Yamaha, Volvo Penta) and BoatUS guidance.
marine.note: Plan on the 1/3 out, 1/3 back, 1/3 reserve fuel rule. Marine tank capacities are usable gallons.

offroad.basis: Multipliers on gallons per hour at normal trail pace; rule-of-thumb values from OEM spec sheets and trail-riding reports.

lore_brindlemere.title: Brindlemere
lore_brindlemere.content: Brindlemere is a market town of about eight hundred people where the high road meets the Wend ferry. It was chartered four hundred and twelve years ago and has never been large or poor. Its farmers sell grain and apples, its smiths make hinges and chain, and its ferry connects the town to the far drovers' road.

lore_wend.title: The River Wend
lore_wend.content: The Wend is slow and brown in summer and fast and brown in spring. It has flooded the lower town twice in living memory, most badly thirty years ago, when it took the old bridge and half the mill lane. The ferry crosses where the river is widest and calmest, a little above the mill.

lore_market_square.title: Market Square
lore_market_square.content: Market Square is paved with river cobbles and centered on a stone well that is older than the town's records. Marketday is the fourth day of the week; stalls go up before dawn and come down by evening. Disputes between stallholders are settled by the reeve, usually within the hour.

lore_kettle.title: The Crooked Kettle
lore_kettle.content: The Crooked Kettle is the only inn in Brindlemere, and it has been the town's living room for longer than anyone alive can say. The ale is honest, the stew is better than it has any right to be, and the innkeeper's gossip is free. Six beds upstairs cost eight bits a night; the stable yard costs four.

lore_reeves_hall.title: Reeve's Hall
lore_reeves_hall.content: Reeve's Hall is where the town does its business: tolls are counted, disputes heard, and the year's accounts read aloud at Founders' Day. On the wall behind the long table hangs the framed Charter, the document that makes Brindlemere a town rather than a village and which every child is taken to see once.

lore_charter.title: The Charter
lore_charter.content: The Charter of Brindlemere was granted four hundred and twelve years ago. It gave the settlement its market, freed it from the lord's tithes, and made the reeve answerable only to the townsfolk. Everyone knows the Charter hangs in Reeve's Hall; few have read it past the first paragraph.

lore_chapel.title: The Chapel of the Quiet Bell
lore_chapel.content: The chapel's square tower holds a bronze bell that has not rung in thirty years. The town calls it the Quiet Bell. Some say the Great Flood cracked it; others say the bell was never cracked at all. Sister Ilsabet keeps the chapel spotless and the bell polished, and she answers questions about it with a small, patient smile.

lore_great_flood.title: The Great Flood
lore_great_flood.content: Thirty years ago the Wend rose in a night and took the old bridge, the mill lane and a dozen cottages. No one in Brindlemere drowned, which the town credits to Brother Anselm, the chapel's keeper at the time, who went door to door in the dark and then, people say, ordered the bell silenced. He died the following spring.

lore_forge.title: Dunmore's Forge
lore_forge.content: Three generations of Dunmores have worked this forge. Marta is the current smith. She makes hinges, nails and knives for the market, and she forged the great chain that holds the ferry to its rope. A bench by the door is the unofficial parliament of the town.

lore_mill.title: Wend Mill
lore_mill.content: Wend Mill has ground the vale's grain for longer than anyone remembers. The Tambers have run it for four generations. Its runner stone cracked at the start of this week; until a new one is found and set, the town's bread comes from last month's flour.

lore_ferry.title: The Wend Ferry
lore_ferry.content: The ferry is a flat boat hauled along a rope. It runs from dawn to evening, carries twelve people or a loaded cart, and closes in a storm. Tamsin Reed has run it for twenty-six years, with her nephew Pip. A crossing is two bits for a person and six for a horse or cart.

lore_far_bank.title: The Far Bank Waystation
lore_far_bank.content: A lonely stone house on the far side of the Wend where drovers and pilgrims wait for the ferry. Bram Hesketh has kept it since his wife died, with his daughter Nessa. The lamp in the window is lit every night so the ferry knows someone is waiting.

lore_quarry.title: Hollin Quarry
lore_quarry.content: Above the old apple terraces lies a grassed-over quarry where the town's first millstones were cut. Nobody has quarried there for generations, but rough blocks and half-finished stones lie in the nettles where the cutters left them.

lore_hollis.title: Reeve Hollis Garrow
lore_hollis.content: Hollis Garrow has been reeve for eleven years. He is careful, fair in small matters and tidy in his accounts, and he takes the town's debts personally. People respect him; they seldom ask what he is thinking.

lore_tamsin.title: Tamsin Reed
lore_tamsin.content: Tamsin Reed is the ferrywoman. She is blunt, dependable and unimpressed by weather, wealth or titles. She says she can smell a storm an hour before it breaks and has been right so often that the town sets its clocks by her.

lore_joss.title: Joss Tamber
lore_joss.content: Joss Tamber is floury, gloomy and generous in equal parts. He gives credit he cannot afford and complains about it cheerfully. When the wheel is still he is hard to be around; when it turns, he sings.

lore_marta.title: Marta Dunmore
lore_marta.content: Marta Dunmore is the town's blacksmith. She is quick, dry-witted and has forgotten more about metal than most people learn. She keeps a handcart in the forge yard that she lends to anyone she trusts, and she is a better judge of trust than the reeve.

lore_ilsabet.title: Sister Ilsabet Vane
lore_ilsabet.content: Sister Ilsabet has kept the chapel for twenty-two years. She is small, calm and impossible to rush. Children bring her their questions and adults bring her their secrets; she has been asked about the bell more often than anyone else in town and has never given the same answer twice.

lore_wren.title: Wren Aldous
lore_wren.content: Wren Aldous learned herb-lore from her grandmother and has been healing Brindlemere's coughs, cuts and fevers ever since. She charges what people can pay. She talks quickly, listens carefully and knows which of her neighbours are quietly struggling.

lore_odo.title: Odo Kettleby
lore_odo.content: Odo Kettleby is the innkeeper of the Crooked Kettle. Round, cheerful and always at work, he is the town's best source of news and its worst keeper of secrets. People who want something told quickly tell it to Odo.

lore_reaping_feast.title: The Reaping Feast
lore_reaping_feast.content: The Reaping Feast falls on the first day of Reapmoon. The whole town gathers at the Crooked Kettle for the harvest supper, the first barrel of the new ale and a great many toasts. No one works that day, and old quarrels are traditionally put aside until the morning after.

lore_pip.title: Pip Marlow
lore_pip.content: Pip Marlow is Tamsin's nephew, fifteen years old, lanky and always coiling rope. He works the ferry every day it runs. Pip hears more than he repeats, and the town's children say he can tell when someone is lying by the way they hold their hands.

lore_bram.title: Bram Hesketh
lore_bram.content: Bram Hesketh keeps the Far Bank Waystation. A quiet widower with a weathered face and a patient manner, he lights the lamp every night so travellers know someone is waiting. His daughter Nessa, eight, is the reason he rarely leaves the house.

lore_calendar.title: The Brindlemere calendar
lore_calendar.content: The year has thirteen moons of twenty-eight days, and every moon starts on Hearthday. The weeks run Hearthday, Plowday, Wellday, Marketday, Tollday, Restday and Feastday. Goldmoon is the eighth moon, Reapmoon the ninth, and the last moon, Longnight, ends the year in a day-long festival.

currency.label: Brindlemere coin
currency.note: A labourer earns about 16 bits a day; a loaf is 1 bit, a night's bed 8, a riding horse about 8 crowns.
